slides.0.title: Winemaking styles in depth
slides.0.subtitle: Chenin, Pinotage, Cap Classique
slides.1.title: The Chenin Blanc style spectrum
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Fresh dry to barrel-fermented
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The same grape ranges from fresh, unoaked wines to rich barrel-fermented ones from dryland old vines; old vines in the Swartland and Olifants River (such as Sadie's Skurfberg) are examples
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Straw wine
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Mullineux and De Trafford make straw wines from Chenin Blanc
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Sparkling and distilling
slides.1.highlights.2.content: In 1971 Frans Malan of Simonsig made Kaapse Vonkel from Chenin Blanc, the start of South African traditional-method sparkling (released commercially in 1973)
slides.1.content: When describing Chenin styles, cover both the vineyard (age, dryland) and the winery (oak, residual sugar).
slides.2.title: Pinotage
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Origin
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Pinot Noir × Cinsaut, crossed by Abraham Perold in the 1920s; the first barrel was made in 1941 and it first appeared on a label in 1961
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Where it is grown
slides.2.highlights.1.content: About 7.6% of area in 2025 (6,619 ha); Pinotage was about 11% of Stellenbosch bottlings in 2022
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Cape Blend
slides.2.highlights.2.content: A South African-style blend of Pinotage with Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah and others; the minimum share is defined differently, so no proportion is examined
slides.2.content: Pinotage ranges from light and fruity to oaky and rich; describe it through vineyard site, vine age and extraction.
slides.3.title: Cap Classique rules
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Current minimums
slides.3.highlights.0.content: At least 12 months on the lees (from the 2023 vintage, previously nine), whole-bunch pressing with cuvée only, and at least 3 bar of bottle pressure (finished wines typically around 6 bar)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Any variety
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Any variety is technically permitted; the CCPA encourages Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier and Chenin Blanc
slides.3.highlights.2.title: The industry
slides.3.highlights.2.content: The CCPA and the Cap Classique name both date from 1992; in autumn 2022 the CCPA had 104 members covering about 95% of traditional-method production; about 80% is consumed in South Africa
slides.3.content: Dosage (typically 6–8 g/L) is a common range, not a legal cap; the ageing minimum has old and new rules, so cite the year.
slides.4.title: Diploma depth: winemaking decisions for Chenin Blanc
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Fresh style: keep the fruit
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Machine or bulk picking, cool stainless-steel fermentation, no MLF, early bottling → apple, guava, tropical fruit and crisp acidity at accessible prices: the backbone of export volume
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Rich style: texture and ageing
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Low-yielding old vines, hand picking, whole-bunch pressing, wild yeast, fermentation in older barrels and lees stirring → waxy, honeyed, nutty character and a broader palate; Chenin’s high acidity keeps tension and ageing potential
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Residual sugar and sweet wines
slides.4.highlights.2.content: The same grape can keep a little residual sugar to balance acidity, or become a straw wine or Noble Late Harvest; Chenin’s acidity keeps sweet wines from cloying, just as in the Loire’s Vouvray and Coteaux du Layon
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Matching style to price
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Fresh styles mostly go to volume retail and bulk, rich old-vine styles to premium bottles; one South African variety spans the whole price ladder, a good example for essays on how varietal versatility supports an industry
